entry.evidence: The train signal deconvolutions showed a clear P-wave travel-time reduction from mid July to the beginning of September 2015

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML full text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: Reused the authors' earlier train-signal extraction and deconvolution-interferometry processing for the SDM-1 borehole array, applied to two 5-month deployments in 2015.
steps.quote: extracted the train signals as described in a previous study12

steps.action: Observed a P-wave travel-time reduction of up to about 0.7 ms from mid July to early September 2015 for all geophone pairs that include geophone 10, and not for other pairs.
steps.quote: The train signal deconvolutions showed a clear P-wave travel-time reduction

steps.action: Checked for a geophone shift by applying deconvolution interferometry to high-frequency acoustic waves in the borehole fluid (Supplement Section 2); these showed no associated travel-time change.
steps.quote: To check if a geophone shift could cause the apparent P-wave travel-time changes

steps.action: Hypothesized that the gas-water contact rose: geophone 10 is the only geophone below the GWC, and gas-to-water substitution would raise P speed and shorten travel times.
steps.quote: An upward movement of the GWC would replace gas by water in the porous sandstone

steps.action: Dated the anomaly from July 17 to September 3 (Fig. 3a) and noted that this span roughly matched the reservoir drilling of well ZRP-3, 4.5 km away.
steps.quote: It was found that this time span approximately matched the drilling of the reservoir of well ZRP-3

steps.action: S-wave interferometry between geophone pairs failed because of poor signal-to-noise ratio, so the authors built a reversed receiver-function approach: horizontal-by-vertical deconvolution (HZdecon) at single geophones to retrieve P-to-S converted waves (Supplement Section 3).
steps.quote: This was not feasible because the S-wave responses, obtained by deconvolution of the horizontal components between geophone pairs, had a poor signal-to-noise ratio.

steps.action: Measured time shifts of the PS wavelet from the anhydrite layer at geophone 10 by cross-correlating it with the deployment average; a shift appears from mid July to early September, and none at the upper geophones.
steps.quote: the HZdecon responses of geophone 10 showed a time shift from mid July to the beginning of September

steps.action: Compared the anticorrelated P decrease (about 0.7 ms) and PS delay increase (about 1 ms, implying an S travel-time increase of about 0.3 ms) with the GWC-rise prediction (P velocity up, S velocity slightly down).
steps.quote: The observations support the hypothesis of a rise of the gas-water contact

steps.action: Analysed 5-30 Hz ambient noise power at geophones 8 and 10: geophone 10 is quieter from July 17 00 h to September 2 19 h, which timed the anomaly precisely (Figs. 3c, 4); a nearby micro-earthquake was noted at onset (Supplement Section 4).
steps.quote: During this period the noise level of geophone 10 is clearly lower.

steps.action: Estimated the GWC elevation (about 23 m) from the 0.7 ms P travel-time decrease, using sonic-log P velocities above and below the GWC (3321 and 3688 m/s; Supplement Section 5) instead of a full Gassmann calculation.
steps.quote: a 0.7 ms P-wave travel-time decrease would correspond to an elevation of the GWC by 23 m

steps.action: Checked that a 23 m GWC rise also accounts for the PS delay increase, implying a realistic 52 m/s (2.6%) S-velocity decrease from the density increase.
steps.quote: [...] if this elevation of the GWC could also explain the increase in the PS delay time

steps.action: Posed the question of what caused the GWC elevation.
steps.quote: the question arises what caused the elevation of the GWC

steps.action: Excluded gas production as the cause: regional production data show no correlation with the anomaly.
steps.quote: The gas production data in the area were checked, but do not show a correlation [...] .

steps.action: Obtained NAM's detailed ZRP-3 drilling report and reconstructed the timeline: reservoir reached July 13, mud losses July 18-19, GWC depth July 31, cementing August 28-29, well left August 30.
steps.quote: we investigated the detailed drilling report that was provided by NAM

steps.action: Excluded two rivals. Drilling noise: drilling intervals are scattered, and noise would affect all geophone pairs (Fig. S3). Mud losses: they began 30 h after the anomaly started.
steps.quote: Thus, drilling noise cannot explain the observations.

steps.action: Proposed that pore-pressure variations caused by drilling at ZRP-3 drove the anomaly, using NAM static bottom-hole pressure data (BHPs = ρm g h).
steps.quote: A more likely cause is the pore pressure variations caused by drilling.

steps.action: Compared static BHP at ZRP-3 (36 to 39 MPa rise, July 23 to August 19) with the seismic time series: anticorrelated with P travel time and correlated with PS delay (Fig. 3a,b).
steps.quote: The gradual trend of increasing BHP is anti-correlated with the P-wave travel-time decrease from geophone 8 to 10

steps.action: Converted the 23 m GWC rise to about 0.23 MPa of pore-pressure increase. Computed pressure-front delays: 3 days 7-16 h from drilling into the Ten Boer claystone to anomaly onset, and 3 days 11.5-19 h from cement hardening to anomaly end.
steps.quote: we calculated the time that the pressure front took to propagate from ZRP-3 to SDM-1

steps.action: Designed a test of whether pore-pressure diffusion can account for the observed delay over 4.5 km.
steps.quote: it should be verified that the process of pore pressure diffusion can explain the time delay

steps.action: Estimated hydraulic diffusivity from the delay times, assuming isotropic spherical diffusion (r = sqrt(4πDt)), giving 4.9-5.7 m2/s.
steps.quote: The pore pressure diffusivity is estimated from the propagation time of the pressure front

steps.action: Made an independent diffusivity estimate from literature material properties via poroelastic modulus (Method §5 ¶1: k = 120 mD, φ = 0.15, Kd = 11 GPa, µd = 9.7 GPa), giving 3.9 m2/s. Matching the seismic range needs 151-176 mD, within the reported 1-1000 mD.
steps.quote: An independent estimate of the hydraulic diffusivity (D) can be calculated from the material properties

steps.action: Concluded that pore-pressure diffusion in the water-bearing reservoir can explain the delay between drilling overpressure and the GWC change.
steps.quote: Thus, it is concluded that pore pressure diffusion in the water-bearing part of the reservoir can explain the time delay

steps.action: Faced with a 150 m offset fault between the wells that should hinder diffusion, the authors added an auxiliary: a speculative high-permeability conduit, possibly two linked ENE-WSW fault segments (Fig. 5a).
steps.quote: suggest a high permeability conduit between the two locations

steps.action: Refined the mechanism: the pressure front lifted the brine column in the open, perforated SDM-1 well, elevating the GWC near the well.
steps.quote: Our speculative hypothesis is that the pressure front, caused by overpressure at the remote well head

steps.action: Kept the drilling-linked interpretation as the only plausible explanation found, while acknowledging that parts are highly speculative.
steps.quote: we were unable to find another plausible explanation

tree.answer: Yes: a transient 1.5-month travel-time anomaly confined to geophone 10
No: GWC change and pore pressure are inferred from travel times and noise
Explain the cause of the anomaly
Yes: geophone shift, gas production, drilling noise, mud losses, drilling pore pressure
Partly: Gassmann sign of P/S changes, timing, and all-pair versus single-pair effects
Found: one live drilling event recorded passively

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No: a single event, not repeated
Partly: three observables agree and an independent diffusivity estimate is similar
No review file supplied; four reviewers are acknowledged

end.claim: Transient P and PS travel-time changes at SDM-1 reflect a temporary rise of the gas-water contact caused by pore-pressure diffusion (D about 5 m2/s) from drilling of ZRP-3, 4.5 km away.

decisive_move.sentence: Matching the anomaly's timing and trend to the ZRP-3 drilling timeline and bottom-hole pressure links the GWC change to distant drilling.

gates.evidence: The geophone data were recorded for seismicity monitoring and analysed for compaction before the anomaly was seen. The drilling report and BHP data were sought only after the timing match (§3.2 ¶1). The GWC hypothesis risked failure on the sign of the PS change and on the independent diffusivity estimate (§2.2 ¶3, §3.3 ¶4). Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: NAM drilling report and static bottom-hole pressure records for ZRP-3
Poroelastic modulus and hydraulic diffusivity formula D = Nk/η
Passing trains used as repetitive seismic sources

novelty_claims.quote: an effect that is unexpected and may be important for other drilling activities
recordings of deep borehole geophone arrays, deployed for monitoring seismicity at depth as in this case, can be used to detect changes in material properties

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: GWC elevation about 23 m (estimate_with_resolution, which the authors call only indicative, with large uncertainty); diffusivity 4.9-5.7 m2/s (estimate_with_resolution); borehole arrays with train noise can monitor velocity changes (capability_characterized); the fault-conduit and brine-column mechanisms are speculative hypotheses that were not tested. The noise-level reduction at geophone 10 is left unexplained. The evidence is a single event, with no replication at other wells or times. The link to drilling rests on timing and correlation. Inference: the drilling relation was identified after the anomaly was seen, so the timing match is post hoc. Supplementary material was not supplied, so the checks reported there (Sections 1-5, Fig. S3) are coded from main-text descriptions only. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

alternatives_considered.reason: S-wave responses had poor signal-to-noise ratio

alternatives_considered.chosen: Sonic-log P velocities above and below the GWC
alternatives_considered.reason: Local moduli unknown; rough estimates would have large uncertainties

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Gas production; drilling noise; downhole mud losses
alternatives_considered.reason: No correlation with gas production; drilling noise would affect all pairs and is scattered in time; mud losses began 30 h after anomaly onset
